KATHMANDU, Nepal (CNN) -- Nepal's government ordered the country's army chief of staff fired Sunday, touching off street protests and a split in Nepal's Maoist-dominated ruling coalition. General Rookmangud Katawal gestures after inspecting the guard of honour in New Delhi on December 12, 2007. But Gen. Rookmangud Katawal has refused to accept his dismissal, and Nepalese President Ram Baran Yadav -- the constitutional commander-in-chief of the country's armed forces -- has told Katawal to remain in office, a presidential spokesman said. Nepal's Cabinet voted to dismiss Katawal after the military refused the government's order to stop recruiting about 3,000 new soldiers to fill vacant positions when it has yet to take in former Maoist rebels, as a 2006 peace deal required. The move prompted the Maoists' largest coalition partner to quit the government, the party's leader said. "Without consensus, the ongoing peace process will not reach its logical conclusion and the drafting of the new constitution will not be possible," said Ishwor Pokharel, general secretary of the Communist Party of Nepal (Unified Marxist-Leninist). "The consensus that existed so far has come to standstill." Supporters of both sides in the dispute took to the streets for demonstrations Sunday. Despite sporadic clashes between the two factions, there were no serious injuries reported. The Maoists laid down their arms and won power in 2008 elections after an agreement that ended a decade-long insurgency. Under the deal, more than 19,000 former insurgents were to be integrated into the country's security forces. But two weeks ago, the government asked Katawal to explain why he went to the Supreme Court to challenge the government's refusal to extend the tenure of eight brigadier generals in March. Government spokesman Krishna Bahadur Mahara said Sunday that the government was not satisfied with Katawal's explanation and fired him -- three months before his scheduled retirement -- in a meeting that the Maoists' coalition partners boycotted. Pokharel said his party urged the Maoists not to fire Katawal without a consensus in the country's parliament. He said the Maoists, led by Prime Minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal, ignored that advice. "We do not like the way the Maoists' way of functioning," Pokharel said. The Maoists hold 238 of the 601 seats in parliament, while Pokharel's party has 109. The Maoists could continue to hold power with the support of smaller parties, but Pokharel said his party is working to form a new ruling coalition. The Cabinet named an interim army chief, but presidential spokesman Rajendra Dahal told CNN that 18 parties in Nepal's parliament asked Yadav to keep Katawal on the job. There was no immediate reaction from the government on the president's decision.

**KATHMANDU, Nepal (CNN) —** Nepal’s government ordered the dismissal of the country’s army chief of staff on Sunday, triggering street protests and a split within the Maoist-dominated ruling coalition.

Gen. Rookmangud Katawal gestures after inspecting the guard of honor in New Delhi on December 12, 2007.

Katawal, however, has refused to accept his dismissal. Nepalese President Ram Baran Yadav—the constitutional commander-in-chief of the country’s armed forces—has instructed him to remain in office, according to a presidential spokesman.

Nepal’s Cabinet voted to dismiss Katawal after the military defied a government order to halt the recruitment of about 3,000 new soldiers to fill vacant positions, despite having yet to incorporate former Maoist rebels as required under a 2006 peace agreement.

The decision prompted the Maoists’ largest coalition partner to withdraw from the government, the party’s leader said.

“Without consensus, the ongoing peace process will not reach its logical conclusion and the drafting of the new constitution will not be possible,” said Ishwor Pokharel, general secretary of the Communist Party of Nepal (Unified Marxist-Leninist). “The consensus that existed so far has come to a standstill.”

Supporters of both sides in the dispute took to the streets on Sunday. Despite sporadic clashes between the two factions, no serious injuries were reported.

The Maoists laid down their arms and won power in the 2008 elections following an agreement that ended a decade-long insurgency. Under the deal, more than 19,000 former insurgents were to be integrated into the country’s security forces.

Two weeks ago, however, the government asked Katawal to explain why he had petitioned the Supreme Court to challenge its March decision not to extend the tenures of eight brigadier generals.

Government spokesman Krishna Bahadur Mahara said Sunday that the government was dissatisfied with Katawal’s explanation and dismissed him—three months before his scheduled retirement—during a meeting boycotted by the Maoists’ coalition partners.

Pokharel said his party had urged the Maoists not to dismiss Katawal without reaching a consensus in the country’s parliament. He said the Maoists, led by Prime Minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal, ignored that advice.

“We do not like the Maoists’ way of functioning,” Pokharel said.

The Maoists hold 238 of parliament’s 601 seats, while Pokharel’s party holds 109. The Maoists could remain in power with the support of smaller parties, but Pokharel said his party was working to form a new ruling coalition.

The Cabinet appointed an interim army chief, but presidential spokesman Rajendra Dahal told CNN that 18 parties represented in Nepal’s parliament had asked Yadav to keep Katawal in his post.

The government did not immediately respond to the president’s decision.

KATHMANDU, Nepal (CNN) — Nepal’s government dismissed the head of the national army on Sunday, triggering street demonstrations and fracturing the country’s Maoist-led governing alliance.

Gen. Rookmangud Katawal—seen gesturing after reviewing an honor guard in New Delhi on December 12, 2007—rejected the decision to remove him. Presidential spokesman Rajendra Dahal said President Ram Baran Yadav, Nepal’s constitutional commander in chief, instructed Katawal to continue serving in his post.

The Cabinet decided to oust Katawal after the army defied a government directive to suspend the recruitment of roughly 3,000 soldiers for vacant posts. The military had not yet incorporated former Maoist fighters, as stipulated by a 2006 peace agreement.

In response to the dismissal, the Maoists’ biggest coalition ally withdrew from the government, according to its leader.

Ishwor Pokharel, general secretary of the Communist Party of Nepal (Unified Marxist-Leninist), warned that the peace process could not be brought to a proper conclusion, nor could a new constitution be drafted, without political agreement. He said the consensus that had existed until then had broken down.

Demonstrators supporting both camps gathered in the streets on Sunday. Although the rival groups clashed sporadically, no major injuries were reported.

After a peace accord ended a decade of insurgency, the Maoists surrendered their weapons and emerged victorious in the 2008 elections. The agreement called for more than 19,000 former rebels to be absorbed into Nepal’s security services.

Two weeks before Katawal’s dismissal, the government demanded that he justify his decision to petition the Supreme Court over its March refusal to extend the terms of eight brigadier generals.

Government spokesman Krishna Bahadur Mahara said Sunday that officials found Katawal’s response inadequate and removed him during a Cabinet session boycotted by the Maoists’ coalition allies. Katawal was fired three months before he was due to retire.

Pokharel said his party had pressed the Maoists not to dismiss the general unless they first secured agreement in Parliament. Prime Minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal and his Maoist party disregarded that recommendation, he added.

“We do not approve of the way the Maoists operate,” Pokharel said.

The Maoists control 238 seats in Nepal’s 601-member Parliament, compared with 109 held by Pokharel’s party. While the Maoists could remain in government with backing from smaller parties, Pokharel said his party was seeking to assemble a new governing coalition.

Although the Cabinet appointed an acting army chief, Dahal told CNN that 18 parliamentary parties had asked President Yadav to retain Katawal. The government did not immediately respond to the president’s action.

Nepal’s Maoist-led government dismissed army chief Gen. Rookmangud Katawal after months of tension over military recruitment, promotions, and civilian control of the armed forces. The cabinet accused Katawal of repeatedly ignoring government instructions, including an order to halt the recruitment of new soldiers while former Maoist combatants remained in United Nations-monitored camps awaiting decisions on their integration and rehabilitation. The army chief was also criticized for disputes involving the retirement of senior officers and the military’s participation in national sporting events.

Katawal refused to accept the dismissal, arguing that the government had not followed proper constitutional procedures. President Ram Baran Yadav, Nepal’s ceremonial head of state and constitutional commander-in-chief, then instructed him to remain in office. The government had named Lt. Gen. Kul Bahadur Khadka as acting army chief, leaving the country with competing claims over who controlled the military.

The president’s intervention deepened an already serious political crisis. Maoist supporters took to the streets, accusing Yadav and opposition parties of undermining elected civilian authority and protecting the army from democratic oversight. Critics of the Maoists, however, said the dismissal was an attempt to bring the military under party control and warned that it could destabilize the security forces.

The confrontation also fractured the governing coalition. The Communist Party of Nepal–Unified Marxist Leninist, one of the Maoists’ most important coalition partners, withdrew its support, depriving the government of a secure parliamentary majority. Other parties called for a broader political agreement and warned that unilateral action by either the cabinet or the president could damage Nepal’s fragile constitutional order.

At the center of the dispute was the unfinished transformation of Nepal’s security institutions following the end of the decade-long civil war. Under the 2006 peace agreement, the Maoists ended their insurgency, placed thousands of former People’s Liberation Army fighters in cantonments, and entered mainstream politics. The agreement envisioned the integration or rehabilitation of eligible former combatants, but political parties and the army remained deeply divided over how that process should be carried out.

The standoff therefore threatened more than the survival of the government. It put at risk the political consensus that had sustained the peace process, raised fears of renewed confrontation between the Maoists and the army, and further delayed the work of drafting a new constitution. Unless Nepal’s parties reached a compromise over civilian authority, military command, and the future of former Maoist fighters, the crisis risked undermining the democratic transition that began with the 2006 peace settlement.

counterfactuals.output:
**BREAKING NEWS — NEPAL GOVERNMENT DISMISSES ARMY CHIEF, TRIGGERING POLITICAL CRISIS**

**KATHMANDU, Nepal** — Nepal has been plunged into a political crisis after the Maoist-led government moved to dismiss army chief Gen. Rookmangud Katawal, escalating a long-running dispute over control of the military and the integration of former Maoist fighters.

Prime Minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal, the former rebel commander known as Prachanda, accused Katawal of defying government orders. The army chief denied wrongdoing.

The decision immediately divided Nepal’s governing coalition. President Ram Baran Yadav rejected the dismissal and instructed Katawal to remain in his post, setting up a confrontation over the constitutional powers of the prime minister and president.

Several coalition partners opposed the government’s action, arguing that removing the army chief without broad political agreement threatened Nepal’s fragile peace process. Dahal subsequently announced his resignation, saying the president’s intervention was unconstitutional.

The dispute centers partly on plans to integrate thousands of former Maoist combatants into Nepal’s security forces — a key provision of the 2006 peace agreement that ended a decade-long insurgency. Military leaders and opposition parties have resisted large-scale integration, warning that it could politicize the army.

The Maoists emerged as the largest party in Nepal’s 2008 elections after abandoning armed struggle and entering mainstream politics. But tensions between the former rebels, the military and traditional political parties have remained high.

Security was tightened in Kathmandu amid fears of protests and prolonged political instability. Analysts warn that the standoff could delay implementation of the peace accord and the drafting of a new constitution.

There were no immediate reports of violence, but Nepal now faces renewed uncertainty as political parties attempt to form another government and resolve the confrontation over civilian control of the army.

President Ram Baran Yadav rejected the dismissal and ordered Katawal to remain in command, arguing that the government had not followed proper constitutional and political procedures. Dahal denounced the president’s intervention as unconstitutional and, after coalition partners withdrew their support, resigned on May 4.

The confrontation brought down the Maoist-led government, deepened mistrust between the Maoists and the traditional army, and exposed ambiguities in Nepal’s interim constitution over the powers of the president, prime minister, and military during the post-civil-war transition. Madhav Kumar Nepal subsequently became prime minister.

counterfactuals.output:
## Nepal’s dismissal of army chief opens constitutional and political crisis

**KATHMANDU, Nepal —** Nepal’s Maoist-led Cabinet dismissed army chief Gen. Rookmangud Katawal after months of confrontation over military recruitment, the retirement of senior officers and the proposed integration of former Maoist fighters into the national army. But Katawal refused to step down after President Ram Baran Yadav ordered him to remain in command, turning a dispute over civilian control of the military into a wider constitutional crisis.

The Cabinet, led by Prime Minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal — better known by his nom de guerre, Prachanda — decided on May 3, 2009, to remove Katawal. The government accused the general of repeatedly defying civilian authority and asked the second-ranking officer, Lt. Gen. Kul Bahadur Khadka, to serve as acting army chief.

Katawal, however, continued to report for duty. His position was strengthened late that night when Yadav sent him a letter instructing him to remain in office. The president said the Cabinet’s action lacked the political consensus required during Nepal’s fragile transition from monarchy and civil war.

### A long-running struggle over control of the army

The confrontation had developed over several issues that went to the heart of Nepal’s postwar settlement.

The Maoists, who had fought the state in a decade-long insurgency that ended in 2006, argued that Katawal had ignored government instructions and acted as though the army were beyond civilian control. Among the main accusations were that the army:

- continued recruiting thousands of soldiers despite government objections and a United Nations-monitored peace process;
- resisted the integration of qualified former Maoist combatants into the security forces, as contemplated by the peace agreement;
- sought to retain eight brigadier generals whom the Defense Ministry said should retire; and
- withdrew army athletes from national sporting events after former Maoist fighters were allowed to participate.

To the Maoists, these incidents demonstrated that the army leadership remained loyal to the old political establishment and was obstructing the transformation promised after the end of King Gyanendra’s rule.

Katawal and his supporters denied that he was challenging civilian government. They argued that the army was following existing laws and professional standards. Military leaders also maintained that the mass or politically directed entry of Maoist combatants could undermine the army’s neutrality and chain of command.

The dispute was especially sensitive because the Nepal Army had fought the Maoist People’s Liberation Army during the civil war, which killed more than 13,000 people. Thousands of former rebels were still living in United Nations-supervised cantonments, and their future remained one of the most contentious parts of the peace process.

### Why Katawal refused to leave

Katawal did not accept the Cabinet’s order as final because the president intervened before the dismissal could be fully implemented.

Opposition parties and several members of the governing coalition had urged Yadav to block the removal. They contended that Prachanda had acted without sufficient consultation and that a caretaker-style, consensus-based approach was necessary on a matter involving the national army.

Yadav, whose office was designated under Nepal’s interim constitutional arrangements as the institution associated with supreme command of the army, instructed Katawal to continue performing his duties. The general therefore treated the presidential directive as superseding the Cabinet decision and stayed at army headquarters.

The Maoists rejected that interpretation. They said executive authority belonged to the elected government and accused the president of acting unconstitutionally by countermanding the Cabinet. Constitutional experts were divided because Nepal’s interim charter did not clearly describe how a direct conflict between the president, prime minister and army chief should be resolved.

### Coalition fractures over the dismissal

The decision exposed deep divisions inside Prachanda’s coalition.

The Communist Party of Nepal–Unified Marxist Leninist, or CPN-UML, a crucial coalition partner, opposed removing Katawal without broader agreement. Its ministers boycotted the Cabinet meeting at which the general was dismissed, and the party subsequently withdrew from the government.

Other coalition partners were also reluctant to support the move. Some argued that Katawal had behaved improperly but said firing him abruptly could destabilize the peace process. Parties representing the southern Madhes region were divided, with several leaders warning that the Maoists were attempting to capture state institutions.

The Nepali Congress, the largest opposition party, strongly supported the president’s intervention. It portrayed the dismissal as part of a Maoist effort to bring the army under partisan control. A broad group of non-Maoist parties appealed to Yadav to preserve the existing military command.

The collapse of coalition support left Prachanda without a workable governing majority. On May 4, one day after the Cabinet decision, he resigned as prime minister. In a televised address, he said the president’s action had created “dual power” and undermined the authority of an elected government.

### Rival protests in Kathmandu

The dispute quickly moved from government offices to the streets.

Maoist supporters staged demonstrations condemning Yadav’s order and demanding what they called civilian supremacy over the army. Protesters accused the president of carrying out an unconstitutional political maneuver on behalf of opposition parties and conservative forces. Some burned effigies and blocked roads, while Maoist leaders called strikes and mass rallies.

Opposition activists and civil-society groups held competing demonstrations. They accused the Maoists of authoritarianism and said the attempted dismissal threatened the independence and professionalism of the military. Some welcomed Prachanda’s resignation and praised the president for preventing a unilateral takeover of the army.

Security was tightened around the presidential residence, army headquarters and other key sites in Kathmandu. Although the protests raised fears of renewed confrontation, the army remained in its barracks and did not attempt to seize political power.

### A test for Nepal’s peace process

The crisis revealed how little trust existed among the former combatants and Nepal’s traditional political parties three years after the peace agreement.

For the Maoists, the controversy was evidence that elected civilian leaders could not control institutions inherited from the monarchy. For their opponents, it showed that the former rebels were trying to use their electoral victory to dominate the state while retaining influence over thousands of fighters in cantonments.

Katawal remained army chief under the president’s order and retired at the end of his scheduled term later in 2009. But the confrontation brought down Nepal’s first Maoist-led government and delayed agreements on military reform, constitutional drafting and the rehabilitation or integration of former combatants.

The episode became one of the defining struggles of Nepal’s post-monarchy transition: not simply a dispute over one general, but a battle over who possessed final authority in the new republic and how former enemies would share control of its most powerful institutions.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on the split in Nepal’s Maoist-led ruling coalition following the attempted removal of General Katawal, including relevant quotes, parliamentary seat totals, and background on the 2006 peace agreement.
counterfactuals.output:
## Nepal’s Maoist-led coalition fractures over army chief

Nepal’s governing coalition split in early May 2009 after Prime Minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal—better known by his nom de guerre, **Prachanda**—attempted to remove army chief **General Rookmangud Katawal**.

The Maoist-led cabinet dismissed Katawal on 3 May, accusing him of repeatedly defying civilian authority. The disputes included army recruitment, the extension of service for eight generals and the army’s refusal to participate in sporting events that included former Maoist combatants. Katawal’s supporters argued that the Maoists were trying to politicize the Nepal Army and force the wholesale induction of their former guerrillas.

### Coalition split and presidential intervention

The **Communist Party of Nepal–Unified Marxist Leninist, or CPN-UML**, the coalition’s second-largest party, opposed dismissing Katawal without a broader political consensus. Its ministers withdrew from the cabinet, depriving the Maoists of a dependable parliamentary majority.

President **Ram Baran Yadav** then instructed Katawal to remain in office, effectively overturning the cabinet decision. Prachanda characterized the intervention as unconstitutional and resigned on 4 May.

In his televised resignation, he said:

> “The president’s move is an attack on this infant democracy and the peace process.”

He also declared:

> “I have resigned from the post of prime minister from today to protect democracy and peace.”

The Maoists argued that an unelected military establishment, backed by conservative parties and foreign interests, was obstructing elected civilian authority. Opposition parties countered that the president had prevented the Maoists from gaining control of the national army.

### Parliamentary arithmetic

Nepal’s Constituent Assembly had **601 seats**. The principal party totals following the 2008 election and subsequent nominations were generally reported as:

- **Unified Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist): 229 seats**
- **Nepali Congress: 115**
- **CPN-UML: 108**
- **Madhesi People’s Rights Forum: 54**
- Remaining seats: smaller regional, communist and royalist parties, plus independents

A majority required **301 seats**. The Maoists were therefore the largest party but could not govern alone. Once the UML’s 108 members abandoned the coalition—and other partners hesitated—the government no longer had a secure majority.

Some contemporary reports used slightly different Maoist totals, commonly **220**, because they counted only directly elected and proportional-representation seats, rather than later nominated members or subsequent party changes. The central point remained that the Maoists were well short of a majority by themselves.

## Background: the 2006 peace agreement

The confrontation arose from unresolved provisions of the **Comprehensive Peace Agreement**, signed on **21 November 2006** by the Maoists and Nepal’s multiparty government. That accord ended a decade-long insurgency that had begun in 1996 and killed roughly **13,000 people**—later estimates were higher—and displaced many more.

Under the agreement:

- The Maoists ended their armed rebellion and entered competitive politics.
- The Nepal Army and the Maoist People’s Liberation Army were confined to barracks and UN-monitored cantonments.
- Maoist weapons were stored under United Nations monitoring.
- The parties committed themselves to the **integration and rehabilitation** of eligible former Maoist fighters.
- An elected Constituent Assembly was to write a new constitution and determine the future political order.
- The army was to come under democratic civilian control.

The Maoists subsequently won the largest bloc in the April 2008 Constituent Assembly election, and the assembly abolished Nepal’s monarchy and proclaimed a republic. Prachanda became prime minister in August 2008.

However, the agreement did not specify clearly how many former guerrillas should enter the Nepal Army or on what terms. The United Nations had verified roughly **19,600 Maoist combatants** in cantonments, though thousands were later deemed ineligible or were discharged. Army leaders opposed large-scale or politically organized entry of former rebels, while the Maoists treated integration and “democratization” of the army as central promises of the peace process.

Thus, the Katawal affair was more than a personnel dispute: it exposed unresolved questions over civilian control, presidential authority, the integration of former combatants and whether the Maoists and the old state security establishment trusted one another enough to complete the 2006 settlement.
